reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that team sports scoring evolves as a complex interplay between deterministic skill components and stochastic fluctuations. The scoring event process defines a discrete-time stochastic system where each action leads to a score change. This process is modeled using probabilistic generative frameworks that incorporate both static team skill and dynamic game state influences. Restoration and anti-persistence represent two distinct temporal dependencies in scoring dynamics—restoration implies a tendency toward equilibrium after deviation, whereas anti-persistence reflects momentum-driven persistence. These phenomena are mathematically encoded via conditional probabilities of future scoring given past deviations. The failure mode arises when these assumptions break down due to irregularities in rule enforcement, sudden shifts in team composition, or anomalous external factors. Dualities emerge in how these models can be interpreted either as skill-based or chance-based predictors depending on the regime of observation. For instance, in early-game phases, skill dominates, while late-game scenarios may emphasize chance or fatigue effects. The models must therefore adaptively weight these influences dynamically.
